title: Greenzo

jokes.text: I wear tiger orgasm.
jokes.setup: Liz finds a lipstick in her apartment and shows it around. The owner denies it, saying 'This is sunset blush.'
jokes.punchline: She names her own lipstick shade 'tiger orgasm' with complete nonchalance, as if it's the most normal thing in the world.
jokes.explanation: The joke earns its high score through perfect character integration — only Cerie, the oblivious bombshell, would name a lipstick shade 'tiger orgasm' and not find it worth remarking on. The economy is superb: four words, massive laugh. The deadpan delivery implied by the scripted line is what elevates it. The contrast with the mundane 'sunset blush' is a textbook misdirection-then-subversion structure. Genuinely close to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: The only reason men start taking care of themselves is if they're getting someone to have sex with them. If it wasn't for that, they'd just sit at home in their own filth.
jokes.setup: Liz notices Pete's new hat and spring in his step and suspects an affair.
jokes.punchline: Her sweeping generalization about all men is stated as absolute fact — funny because of its cynical confidence and because it's delivered by someone whose own romantic life is famously sad.
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon observational cynicism — functional and in-character, gets a good chuckle. The sentiment isn't totally novel but the blunt confidence of delivery and the ironic self-unawareness (Liz is also a person who would sit in filth) adds texture.

jokes.text: We're out of string cheese, so I think I'm gonna take off.
jokes.setup: Liz has just delivered her speech about men sitting in their own filth. Pete appears to have been listening the whole time.
jokes.punchline: Pete's non-sequitur exit — anchored entirely on being out of string cheese — perfectly confirms Liz's theory about men while completely ignoring it.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured button on the previous joke. Pete's oblivious response ironically validates Liz's entire thesis without him engaging with it at all. The specificity of 'string cheese' is inspired — it's pathetically mundane. Great economy, great timing.

jokes.text: We're going green, Lemon. And do you know why? To save the earth? So we can drain the remainder of its resources.
jokes.setup: Liz assumes the eco initiative is genuinely about saving the planet.
jokes.punchline: Jack corrects her: the real goal is to drain the remaining resources — a blunt statement of capitalist cynicism presented as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy joke — the setup invites the obvious 'save the earth' answer and then pivots hard to naked corporate greed stated without shame. Perfect character integration; only Jack would say this with pride. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Greenzo is America's first non-judgmental, business-friendly environmental advocate. The free market will solve global warming, if that even exists.
jokes.setup: Jack pitches Greenzo as a green mascot.
jokes.punchline: The tagline undermines its own premise — 'if that even exists' is a perfect corporate hedge appended to a supposedly pro-environment character.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'if that even exists' is the kicker — tacked on so casually it becomes a devastating satirical jab at corporate climate denial. Highly quotable and feels ahead of its time.

jokes.text: Greenzo? Is that the first name that came to your head?
jokes.setup: Jack unveils the name 'Greenzo' with fanfare.
jokes.punchline: Liz's flat skepticism about the name's obviousness is the audience surrogate reaction.
jokes.explanation: Functional audience-surrogate joke. Liz's incredulity is relatable and well-timed but not particularly inventive. The follow-up ('Can you believe it? I mean, it just popped right there') from Jack adds a beat but isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: I'm just so excited about this gig, sir... I haven't worked in a while. My last real job was an ad for Rick Lazio's New York Senate campaign.
jokes.setup: Jared is grateful for the Greenzo role and mentions his last job.
jokes.punchline: His last job was a negative political ad for Rick Lazio (who famously lost to Hillary Clinton), set up as a punchline to his career desperation.
jokes.explanation: Solid topical joke — Rick Lazio is a historically specific choice that rewards politically aware viewers. The joke lands on multiple levels: Jared is a failed actor, and his best work was for a failed political candidate.

jokes.text: Hillary Clinton wants an all-homosexual army. How will that affect my family?
jokes.setup: We flash back to Jared's last job — a political attack ad.
jokes.punchline: The ad is a parody of hysterical right-wing political attack ads, with an absurdly specific and irrelevant accusation delivered in the breathless tones of campaign-ad fearmongering.
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical parody of political attack ad rhetoric — the specificity of 'all-homosexual army' and the earnest 'how will that affect my family?' follow-up is genuinely funny political satire. Good economy, strong absurdist bent.

jokes.text: I just wish my mom were still alive so I could rub it in her fat face.
jokes.setup: Jared is excited about appearing on the Today Show — an ostensibly wholesome achievement.
jokes.punchline: His mother-tribute moment takes a violent and bitter turn: she's dead and he wanted to gloat to her, and he insults her appearance even in death.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The setup lures the audience into expecting a sweet 'I wish my mom could see this' moment — the pivot to 'rub it in her fat face' is a perfectly executed misdirection that reveals Jared's entire character instantly. The 'fat face' detail is gratuitously specific in the best possible way. Highly quotable, rewatch-worthy, excellent structure. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft.

jokes.text: I'm always the only person who shows up.
jokes.setup: Liz explains why she doesn't want to go to Kenneth's party.
jokes.punchline: She's been the lone attendee — a sad, specific detail that's funnier for how matter-of-factly she says it.
jokes.explanation: A good button — the economy of the line is its strength. Reinforces both Liz's loneliness and Kenneth's social isolation without belaboring it.

jokes.text: Happy halloween, baby.
jokes.setup: Tracy arrives in what is presumably a ridiculous Halloween costume.
jokes.punchline: The line implies a wild, over-the-top costume — the joke is entirely visual, with 'baby' adding Tracy's signature flamboyance.
jokes.explanation: We don't know the costume from the transcript, but the context of the episode (it's around Halloween) and Tracy's character makes this a visual gag that rewards the rewatch. The delivery is pure Tracy Jordan.

jokes.text: See, people are like lemmings. Harvey lemmings, my lawyer, who never misses a party.
jokes.setup: Tracy is explaining that people follow crowds like lemmings.
jokes.punchline: He pivots immediately to a specific person named Harvey Lemmings — treating a metaphor as a literal person, with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The structure is near-perfect: Tracy uses a cliché metaphor ('people are like lemmings') and then immediately and sincerely subverts it by referencing an actual person with that surname. The joke works on multiple levels — it's absurdist Tracy logic, it's wordplay, and it reveals that Tracy's world is populated by people with names that match common nouns. The follow-up ('That's not a real person. You made that up.') reaction beat confirms the joke. Highly quotable, strongly in character.

jokes.text: That's not a real person. You made that up.
jokes.setup: Tracy insists Harvey Lemmings his lawyer is real.
jokes.punchline: Liz's flat rebuttal is the straight-man beat that confirms the absurdity of joke 13.
jokes.explanation: The straight-man reaction that sells the Harvey Lemmings joke. Not funny on its own but essential structural support for joke 13.

jokes.text: Kids, you can tell your parents to buy a G.E. front-loading washing machine to save water.
jokes.setup: Greenzo is ostensibly giving eco-friendly tips for kids.
jokes.punchline: The tip is a product placement for G.E. — a blatant corporate sales pitch disguised as environmental advocacy, perfectly undercutting the show's own network parent company.
jokes.explanation: 30 Rock's meta-corporate self-awareness at its best — Greenzo's 'green tip' is nakedly a G.E. product pitch, satirizing both the show and corporate environmentalism simultaneously. Solid craft.

jokes.text: 'Cause if the earth's not here, where else is Greenzo gonna dance?
jokes.setup: Greenzo wraps up his environmental tips.
jokes.punchline: The environmental argument reduces entirely to Greenzo's personal desire to dance — narcissistic non-logic presented as a heartfelt reason.
jokes.explanation: Funny absurdist reduction — the grand cause of environmentalism is narrowed to the most self-serving possible reason. Good economy, and it foreshadows Greenzo's coming ego explosion.

jokes.text: Sorry everybody, that's Meredith Viera.
jokes.setup: Greenzo gloats about what 'Mary' said about him saving the world.
jokes.punchline: He casually name-drops that 'Mary' is Meredith Vieira — either as a humblebrag or because he genuinely calls her Mary — both readings are funny. The meta aspect of NBC talent appearing on a fictional NBC show adds a layer.
jokes.explanation: Greenzo's ego is expanding — calling a famous news anchor by a wrong first name signals his growing delusion. The meta layer (NBC show referencing real NBC talent) is a 30 Rock trademark.

jokes.text: They love him in every demographic. Colored people, broads, fairies, commies. Gosh, we gotta update these forms.
jokes.setup: Jack shares Greenzo's demographic testing data with Liz.
jokes.punchline: Jack rattles off demographic categories using hopelessly outdated and offensive terminology, then acknowledges — without irony about the language itself — only that the forms are out of date.
jokes.explanation: An excellent Jack joke. The character uses slurs from another era with complete confidence, and his only self-correction is the procedural 'we gotta update these forms' — indicating he's bothered by the paperwork inefficiency, not the language. This is a distillation of Jack's character: oblivious privilege stated with boardroom authority. The list builds perfectly and the button lands hard. Genuinely exceptional character integration.

jokes.text: Wow, if you licked the envelope, you could clone him, and then you'd have two Geisses.
jokes.setup: Jack is excited that Don Geiss sent a personal card with a real signature.
jokes.punchline: Liz leaps to the logical absurdist extension — lick the envelope for DNA, clone him — delivered as a throwaway observation.
jokes.explanation: Nice absurdist leap — treating the Geiss mystique so reverently that cloning becomes a genuine option. Good Liz energy, though the follow-up from Jack ('I'm gonna clone Geiss, then compete with a Geiss clone?') is the stronger beat.

jokes.text: Yeah, right, Lemon. I'm gonna clone Geiss, then compete with a Geiss clone for the CEO position? Think it through.
jokes.setup: Liz suggests he could clone Geiss from the envelope.
jokes.punchline: Jack's objection is not that cloning is impossible or unethical — it's the career strategy that concerns him. His only problem with the clone plan is the competitive disadvantage.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The joke works because Jack takes the absurd premise (cloning Geiss) completely seriously — his only objection is strategic, not scientific or ethical. 'Think it through' is a perfect button, delivered with condescension about a cloning scheme. It's pure Jack: corporate logic applied to fantastical scenarios. Strong character integration, excellent economy, highly quotable.

jokes.text: I could make up some excuse, Kenneth, but I have too much respect for you. During your party, I'll be home listening to some Schubert. And, uh, ironically, viewing some Canadian pornography.
jokes.setup: Jack is declining Kenneth's party invitation.
jokes.punchline: Jack frames his refusal as a gesture of respect — giving the 'real' reason. The 'real' reason is Schubert and Canadian pornography. The word 'ironically' is the killer modifier — he's watching Canadian porn as a culturally detached exercise.
jokes.explanation: Among the episode's very best. The joke earns high marks across every dimension. The structure is immaculate: sincere preamble ('I have too much respect for you'), followed by the weirdly specific Schubert-then-Canadian-porn combination. The word 'ironically' applied to pornography is inspired — it implies Jack watches it as a form of cultural anthropology or ironic detachment, which is perfectly and absurdly Jack. Highly quotable, would get a big room reaction. Comparable in craft to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Hope you're ready to party like it's 1999. Which, according to my Bible, will be in seven years.
jokes.setup: Kenneth invites someone to his party using the Prince lyric 'party like it's 1999.'
jokes.punchline: Kenneth reveals his Bible-based timeline places 1999 seven years in the future — implying he follows a literal biblical chronology that puts him in approximately 1992, and he's completely sincere about it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. The structure is perfect: a cultural reference (Prince's 1999) is used naively by Kenneth, who then appends a correction based on his biblical worldview — delivered with complete sincerity and no awareness of its absurdity. The joke reveals Kenneth's fundamentalist religious character with economy and originality. The specificity of 'seven years' (making it 1992 in-universe) is a detail that rewards the math. Near-perfect character integration — this joke could only be Kenneth. Justifiably close to the top of the episode.

jokes.text: That is the body spray that came with my new leather jacket.
jokes.setup: Liz notices a suspicious smell on Pete and asks if he's having an affair.
jokes.punchline: Pete's explanation — a body spray that came with a leather jacket — is specific enough to be plausible but also exactly the kind of midlife crisis purchase that confirms Liz's suspicion.
jokes.explanation: Solid mid-tier joke — the leather jacket/body spray combo is a perfect midlife crisis detail that does double duty (explaining the smell + confirming Pete is going through something). Good economy.

jokes.text: Because you're acting all happy and full of life.
jokes.setup: Pete asks why Liz thinks he's having an affair.
jokes.punchline: Being 'happy and full of life' is framed as suspicious behavior — implying the normal state of marriage/life for Pete is miserable.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy beat — happiness as a red flag for adultery is a cynical but well-executed observational joke that lands with character specificity.

jokes.text: Yeah, and you're married, remember, Pete? Your beautiful wife Paula. And your sons, Robert and Jack. And that creepy little one who's always rubbing himself against the carpet.
jokes.setup: Liz is reminding Pete of his family obligations.
jokes.punchline: The list of Pete's family escalates from normal (wife, sons) to the increasingly specific detail of 'that creepy little one who's always rubbing himself against the carpet' — a perfectly absurd and unsettling detail about one of Pete's children.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. The list begins with warm, specific familial details (wife, sons' names) and builds to the unexpected and deeply weird 'carpet-rubbing' child. The specificity is what makes it — not just 'a weird kid' but a very particular disturbing behavior. The word 'creepy' applied by the observing adult to a child adds a layer of dark comedy. Well-structured, highly quotable, rewatch-worthy.

jokes.text: Oh great, now I smell like midlife crisis!
jokes.setup: Pete and Liz have been arguing; Liz has apparently gotten Pete's body spray on her.
jokes.punchline: Liz treats 'midlife crisis' as a literal scent — the abstract concept of Pete's situation made olfactory.
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical button on the Pete subplot. Making 'midlife crisis' a literal smell is a good absurdist leap, and the line has strong quotability.

jokes.text: Here's a tip, Cerie. Decide what you want before you open the refrigerator. You just released enough hydrofluorocarbons to kill a penguin. This penguin.
jokes.setup: Greenzo catches Cerie browsing the refrigerator with the door open.
jokes.punchline: The lecture escalates from environmental tip to catastrophe — and then the visual kicker of an actual penguin (implied on set) makes the abstract guilt specific and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke with a brilliant visual punchline. The setup is a plausible (if exaggerated) eco-lecture; the escalation to 'kill a penguin' is a funny hyperbole; and then 'this penguin' with an actual penguin present is the perfect absurdist button. The visual gag elevates what would be a good joke to a great one. Strong economy in the punchline — two words ('This penguin') do enormous work.

jokes.text: You ever take off that costume? / You ever take off yours?
jokes.setup: Liz challenges Greenzo about wearing the costume all the time.
jokes.punchline: Greenzo turns it back on Liz — implying she has her own metaphorical costume (her TGS producer persona, her social mask) — followed immediately by 'Greenzo out!' which deflates any profundity.
jokes.explanation: The 'Greenzo out!' tag is the strongest element — it undercuts any pretension in Greenzo's counter and reveals his ego. Good character beat.

jokes.text: Did he just talk to me like I'm ugly?
jokes.setup: Greenzo has just scolded Cerie about the refrigerator.
jokes.punchline: Cerie's reaction is not to the environmental lecture but to the social slight of being spoken to as if she's not attractive — her worldview is entirely organized around her beauty.
jokes.explanation: A fantastic Cerie joke. The entire environmental lecture is processed by Cerie exclusively through the lens of her attractiveness — the thing she took away was a perceived insult to her looks. Perfect character integration; the joke could only work for Cerie. 'Like I'm ugly' is exactly right — not 'talked down to' but specifically 'like I'm ugly.' Highly quotable, great economy.

jokes.text: Hey fellas, I heard a secret about Kenneth's party. Ken went to high school in Georgia with the rapper T.I. And boys... T.I. might show up. But listen... we can't let anyone know. Anyone!
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Grizz and Dotcom a 'secret' with great urgency.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the structure itself — Tracy instructs them not to tell anyone, which is immediately followed by a sequence showing the rumor spreading to literally everyone in New York.
jokes.explanation: The setup for the great gossip montage to follow. Works as a structural joke — the 'don't tell anyone' instruction is obviously futile. Good but the payoff is really the montage sequence.

jokes.text: The gossip-spreading montage — a rapid-fire sequence of bleeped phone calls, text messages, and conversations spreading the T.I. rumor across New York within seconds.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Grizz and Dotcom not to tell anyone about T.I. at Kenneth's party.
jokes.punchline: A bleeped-out rapid montage shows the rumor spreading exponentially — the visual rhythm and the total incomprehensibility of the bleeped content is the comedy.
jokes.explanation: A great structural/visual joke — the escalating montage with bleeped-out content conveys the speed and chaos of rumor-spreading more effectively than any dialogue could. The bleeping is a 30 Rock device that rewards the visual medium. Strong escalation structure.

jokes.text: Well, Kenneth is having this really, really big party.
jokes.setup: The gossip montage culminates in someone prominent spreading the news.
jokes.punchline: The rumor has now reached someone who presents it as established fact — the absurdity that Kenneth's modest party is now citywide news.
jokes.explanation: The landing beat of the gossip montage. Functional cap to the sequence — funny because of the contrast with how the rumor started.

jokes.text: Yes, that's right, you heard me! T.I. is gonna be at Kenneth's party! You're my publicist. Get me in! Oh, also, could you try to kill that story about my mom being meless?
jokes.setup: A celebrity has heard about the party and is calling their publicist.
jokes.punchline: 'My mom being meless' — an incomprehensible but completely confident non-word problem that the celebrity treats as a real PR crisis.
jokes.explanation: The bleeped-out 'meless' is a fun absurdist non-word joke — the content of the celebrity's problem is presumably bleeped for comic effect, leaving only an incomprehensible stub.

jokes.text: I love T.I. Please, respect celebrity privacy.
jokes.setup: Someone claims to love T.I.
jokes.punchline: Immediately follows with 'please respect celebrity privacy' — having just publicly declared love for a celebrity, negating their own call for privacy.
jokes.explanation: Quick ironic beat — decent economy, mild laugh. The self-contradiction is the joke, delivered fast enough to work.

jokes.text: Bob Logan from Texas Instruments is gonna be there? Logan must be in contention for the CEO spot as well.
jokes.setup: Jonathan tells Jack that T.I. is going to be at Kenneth's party.
jokes.punchline: Jack mishears 'T.I.' as 'Texas Instruments' (T.I. is a real company abbreviation) and immediately frames it as a corporate rivalry — a perfect Jack misunderstanding.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The joke works on two levels: it's a wordplay/misdirection joke (T.I. the rapper vs. Texas Instruments) AND a perfect character joke — of course Jack Donaghy would immediately process a hip-hop reference through the lens of corporate competition. His entire worldview filters everything through business. The specificity of 'Bob Logan' as a fabricated rival executive is inspired. Excellent character integration, strong structure.

jokes.text: I, uh, haven't had a chance to get to that Greenzo stuff yet. Hey, did you leave your computer on all night? Yeah, it just takes a really long time to reboot in the morning.
jokes.setup: Greenzo has been lecturing people about wasting energy.
jokes.punchline: Liz left her computer on all night and offers a transparently self-serving excuse — juxtaposed with the episode's green theme.
jokes.explanation: Functional hypocrisy joke — Liz is caught wasting energy while avoiding Greenzo's lectures. The reboot excuse is weak but relatable. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: Hey, you know what else takes a long time? Building a new earth.
jokes.setup: Liz claims her computer just takes a long time to reboot.
jokes.punchline: Greenzo pivots her mundane excuse into an environmental guilt trip with absurd proportions.
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — Greenzo's pivot from 'reboot takes a long time' to 'so does building a new earth' is a nice logical bridge that lands with absurdist weight. Good economy.

jokes.text: You people make me sick. You act like you care, but you do nothing. Do you even bother to compost your own feces?
jokes.setup: Greenzo is upset that people aren't doing enough for the environment.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from reasonable eco-concern to 'compost your own feces' is the turn — it goes from normal advocacy to an extreme and personally invasive demand.
jokes.explanation: The Greenzo-goes-too-far arc is well-executed here. 'Compost your own feces' is a funny escalation point — technically real eco-advice but presented in an unhinged way. Good character work for the Greenzo arc.

jokes.text: Are you saying actors can't change the world? I guess nobody bothered to tell Sharon Stone.
jokes.setup: Liz dismisses Greenzo as 'just an actor.'
jokes.punchline: Greenzo invokes Sharon Stone as the paragon of actor-as-world-changer — a choice that is funny precisely because Sharon Stone is a notably odd choice for this argument.
jokes.explanation: The Sharon Stone reference is the key — it's a specific, odd choice that implies Greenzo's understanding of celebrity activism is slightly off. Good character work, solid economy.

jokes.text: So let's have a little less yappity yap and a little more kity clack.
jokes.setup: Greenzo is telling people to stop talking and start acting on climate change.
jokes.punchline: 'Yappity yap' and 'kity clack' are made-up nonsense words for talking and typing/working — the invented argot of an unhinged environmental mascot.
jokes.explanation: Greenzo's invented vocabulary is funny — 'kity clack' for typing is an odd coinage that lands well. Shows his character degenerating into unhinged mascot behavior.

jokes.text: You jag! I just got this, like, eight years ago.
jokes.setup: Greenzo apparently damages or confiscates Liz's styrofoam cup.
jokes.punchline: 'Eight years ago' — the cup is absurdly old, suggesting Liz has been holding onto a single styrofoam cup for nearly a decade, which is pathetic and specific.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'eight years ago' for a styrofoam cup is a great Liz Lemon detail — she's sentimental about the most mundane objects. Also ironic given the environmental theme.

jokes.text: Good job. Leave all the lights on for the invisible people.
jokes.setup: Greenzo is lecturing about energy waste.
jokes.punchline: 'Invisible people' is an unhinged eco-guilt phrase — the idea that leaving lights on is somehow for ghostly non-existent people is delightfully mad.
jokes.explanation: Greenzo's rhetoric is becoming increasingly unmoored from reality. 'Invisible people' is a good absurdist touch — eco-guilt morphing into something between sarcasm and delusion.

jokes.text: Liz! / Paula? / You're cheating with your wife! Why didn't you tell me about this!
jokes.setup: Liz has been convinced Pete is having an affair. Paula shows up at the apartment.
jokes.punchline: The twist: Pete IS sneaking around — but with his own wife. Liz's accusation ('You're cheating with your wife!') is technically accurate but nonsensical, and her outrage is about being left out of the secret, not the infidelity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff joke. The entire lipstick/affair subplot is resolved with a genuinely funny twist — Pete's 'affair' is with his own wife, and they've been sneaking around for the thrill. 'You're cheating with your wife!' is a perfectly formed paradoxical sentence. The resolution is earned and subverts the setup beautifully. Strong callback value.

jokes.text: That's my fault. I get off on the sneaking around. Who knew, right?
jokes.setup: Liz is shocked that Pete and Paula have been conducting their marriage like an affair.
jokes.punchline: Paula casually admits she's turned on by the secrecy — presenting a completely functional adult kink with a 'who knew?' shrug, as if it's mildly surprising trivia.
jokes.explanation: Strong character beat for a one-scene guest. The breezy confession is well-delivered — the comedy comes from the casual normalization of what is a very specific sexual preference, plus the 'who knew' suggesting genuine self-discovery.

jokes.text: Why is there a pop-tart in the bed? What do you do with the pop-tart?
jokes.setup: Paula finds a pop-tart in the bed — this was mentioned at the very start of the episode.
jokes.punchline: The pop-tart callback — mysterious at the open, now contextualized in Pete and Paula's 'affair' roleplay — suggests acts with the pop-tart too disturbing to contemplate.
jokes.explanation: A well-earned callback. The pop-tart was introduced as a mysterious non-sequitur; its reappearance in the 'cheating with your wife' context makes it suddenly and retroactively disturbing. The question 'What do you do with the pop-tart?' voiced by Paula is the perfect amount of alarm. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: Yeah, and he's gonna perform. / And Fall Out Boy will be there too. / And there's gonna be foxy boxing! / Foxy boxing? I love foxy boxing! It combines my two favorite things: Boxing and referees!
jokes.setup: The T.I. rumor has snowballed and people are adding increasingly wild claims about the party.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's love of foxy boxing is resolved as loving it for 'boxing and referees' — the expected punchline is 'women fighting' but his actual reason is the referees, a completely unexpected and absurd preference.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup ('foxy boxing') creates a clear expectation (Tracy loves it because of attractive women). The subversion — 'boxing and referees' — is completely unexpected and perfectly absurd. It's a great misdirection that also reveals something beautifully weird about Tracy's mind. Only Tracy Jordan would specify referees. Highly quotable and broadly accessible. Strong competitor for the episode's top joke.

jokes.text: You dummy, first of all, you didn't dial that cell phone. Second of all, that is your own rumor.
jokes.setup: Tracy tries to call Harvey Lemmings on his cell phone to get into the party.
jokes.punchline: Liz points out he didn't actually dial, and also that Harvey Lemmings is a rumor Tracy himself started — double stupidity exposed simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Harvey Lemmings while also exposing Tracy's self-defeating scheme. The double correction structure (you didn't dial; it's your own rumor) is economical.

jokes.text: Just like colonial Williamsburg.
jokes.setup: Liz warns that the party will fail expectations.
jokes.punchline: Colonial Williamsburg as an example of expectations not meeting reality is a very specific, very Liz Lemon reference — it implies she went to Colonial Williamsburg, was disappointed, and carries that disappointment.
jokes.explanation: A great throwaway reference — Colonial Williamsburg as the benchmark for disappointing hype is a choice that reveals Liz Lemon's Midwestern nerd experience perfectly. Four words, high specificity, pure character. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Kenneth, thanks for letting my cousins come to your party.
jokes.setup: Tracy is working the situation to get into Kenneth's party.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has apparently already invited his cousins before getting approval — the cousins are presumably visible and numerous.
jokes.explanation: Quick Tracy beat — funny for the presumption but not particularly distinctive.

jokes.text: I'm just horny to be in New York.
jokes.setup: Tracy's cousin is introduced at Kenneth's party.
jokes.punchline: The cousin uses 'horny' in what appears to be a malapropism for 'excited/eager' — either he doesn't know the word's primary slang meaning, or this is accurate and he means exactly what he says.
jokes.explanation: Nice quick double-meaning joke — the ambiguity of whether this is a malapropism or a sincere statement is what makes it land. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Well, before, when I told you I didn't wanna come to your party, I was just kidding! Isn't that a fantastic joke?
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to get himself invited to Kenneth's party after initially turning it down.
jokes.punchline: Jack tries to claim his sincere refusal was a 'joke' — and then asks Kenneth to confirm it's a 'fantastic joke,' putting Kenneth in an uncomfortable position. The joke is on Jack for the desperation.
jokes.explanation: A great character reversal — Jack, who operates from a position of supreme confidence, is now desperately trying to manufacture his own party invitation. 'Isn't that a fantastic joke?' is a wonderful indicator of how uncomfortable his position is. Strong callback.

jokes.text: So that's the way you wanna play this?
jokes.setup: Kenneth demurs, saying Jack doesn't want to come to his 'silly party.'
jokes.punchline: Jack responds to Kenneth's polite brush-off as if it's a power play — treating the most earnest person in the world as a corporate adversary.
jokes.explanation: Jack treating Kenneth's sweet diffidence as a negotiating tactic is a perfect character joke — it's both funny and reveals Jack's inability to interact with the world outside corporate power dynamics.

jokes.text: Sold by our company. [Jack's quiet response to Greenzo's pitch about green technology]
jokes.setup: Greenzo on the Today Show urges people to switch to green technology.
jokes.punchline: Jack's quiet, satisfied 'sold by our company' — monitoring the broadcast — shows his entire reason for supporting the initiative: not environmentalism but sales.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum Jack. The sotto voce 'sold by our company' is a perfect encapsulation of the episode's satirical theme. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: Meredith just taught us a very important lesson, kids. It's rude to interrupt people.
jokes.setup: Meredith Vieira mentions on-air that TVs use power even when off — interrupting Greenzo's segment.
jokes.punchline: Greenzo pivots from the environmental fact to lecturing about manners — using children's programming logic to shut down a journalist, which is both controlling and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — Greenzo's escalating ego leads him to use condescending children's-show logic on a national news anchor. The pivot from environmentalism to etiquette policing reveals his control issues and character degradation.

jokes.text: Wow, is that true? / It doesn't matter if it's true. He works for that money.
jokes.setup: Greenzo claims on TV that global warming could end in 5 years with a 2% tax on the super-rich.
jokes.punchline: Jack's response to whether it's true is 'it doesn't matter if it's true — he works for that money.' Truth is irrelevant; loyalty to donors is the only criterion.
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire — Jack's dismissal of truth in favor of class loyalty is a biting commentary. 'He works for that money' is a concise statement of captured-politics logic. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: I knew we should have gone with Angie Harmon.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz watch Greenzo go off the rails on live TV.
jokes.punchline: Jack's regret is expressed through a specific celebrity alternative — Angie Harmon as the business-friendly environmental advocate they should have chosen. The specificity of the name makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Classic 30 Rock specificity joke — the name 'Angie Harmon' is funnier than any generic celebrity choice would be. The implicit suggestion that Angie Harmon would be more ideologically compliant is its own commentary.

jokes.text: So much hair. / Sorry, she likes me natural.
jokes.setup: Pete has apparently gone full hippie/natural as part of his renewed romance with Paula.
jokes.punchline: Pete apologizes for the hair by explaining his wife's preference — treating excessive body hair as a discovered compatibility.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe/character beat. The visual of Pete with significantly more body hair is the gag; the line explains it efficiently.

jokes.text: Look, Paula and I got married our sophomore year. She was pregnant 20 minutes into the first date.
jokes.setup: Pete is explaining why he and Paula need to use Liz's apartment to rekindle their marriage
jokes.punchline: 'She was pregnant 20 minutes into the first date' — an extraordinary speed of unintended pregnancy that suggests something both comic and alarming
jokes.explanation: '20 minutes into the first date' is a beautifully specific and absurd number. The joke works because of the precision — not 'early' or 'quickly' but exactly 20 minutes, which somehow makes it funnier and more vivid. Good Pete character moment that recontextualizes his entire marriage.

jokes.text: We did it on your kitchen table. I shouldn't have told you that.
jokes.setup: Pete is enthusiastically updating Liz on his revitalized relationship with Paula.
jokes.punchline: Pete overshares that he and Paula had sex on Liz's kitchen table, then immediately recognizes it was TMI — the recognition doesn't undo the damage.
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — the kitchen table is specific enough to be properly gross, and 'I shouldn't have told you that' is a classic overshare button. The meta-recognition doesn't help Liz at all.

jokes.text: Oh hey, could you come home early tonight? Paula wants to get caught again.
jokes.setup: Liz has just agreed to let Pete and Paula use her apartment.
jokes.punchline: Pete immediately makes a request — Liz needs to come home early so Paula can 'get caught,' confirming that Liz's role in their sex life is to provide the excitement of almost being caught.
jokes.explanation: Excellent button on the Pete/Paula subplot. The reveal that Liz's function is to 'catch' them — making her an involuntary prop in their erotic scenario — is a great dark comedy escalation. 'Got it' from Liz implies resigned acceptance, which is perfect. Strong economy, great character work.

jokes.text: While you're out there destroying the earth, I'll be saving it. And history will remember me. When I die, they'll wanna put my face on money. If there were money in the future instead of just hugs.
jokes.setup: Greenzo is going megalomaniacal in his confrontation with Jack.
jokes.punchline: The vision of his face on money is grandiose; the tag 'if there were money in the future instead of just hugs' is the absurdist kicker — implying a future economy based entirely on hugs.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. The joke builds perfectly: face-on-money megalomaniac fantasy, then the absurdist pivot to a hug-based economy. It also satirizes utopian environmentalism (the future will have no money, only love). Highly quotable, great escalation structure, and 'just hugs' is an inspired detail.

jokes.text: You either get on board, or you're gonna wake up on that island with Phil Donahue and the electric car.
jokes.setup: Jack is threatening Greenzo with consequences for going rogue.
jokes.punchline: The threat involves an island where Jack has apparently exiled Phil Donahue and the electric car — two things from the same ideological world, banished together.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Jack joke. The threat of an island populated by liberal icons is Jack's ultimate punishment — Phil Donahue and the electric car as co-exiles is a hilariously specific pairing. It implies Jack has already sent them there. The confident matter-of-factness of the threat is perfect character comedy. Highly quotable, among the episode's very best.

jokes.text: No, I've always been Greenzo. You're crazy.
jokes.setup: Jack reminds Greenzo that he created him.
jokes.punchline: Greenzo denies having an identity before Greenzo — he has fully become the character.
jokes.explanation: Character comedy on Greenzo's complete identity dissolution. Funny because of its commitment — he's not playing along, he genuinely believes it.

jokes.text: Can you fire the wind, Jack? Can you fire a hurricane?
jokes.setup: Jack fires Greenzo.
jokes.punchline: Greenzo's response equates himself with natural phenomena — he cannot be fired because he IS the wind.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable, excellent structure. The rhetorical questions ('Can you fire the wind?') have genuine comedic power — it's the logic of someone who has completely lost the plot, delivered with total conviction. The escalation to 'a hurricane' is a nice build. Very close to 8.5 in craft.

jokes.text: We're developing that technology!
jokes.setup: Greenzo asks if you can fire the wind or a hurricane.
jokes.punchline: Jack takes the rhetorical questions literally — GE is actually developing weather-control technology. The absurdity is treated as a mundane corporate update.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. Greenzo asks 'Can you fire a hurricane?' as a rhetorical flourish — Jack answers 'We're developing that technology' with complete corporate authority, treating weather control as an ongoing R&D project. It's a perfect Jack joke: it takes the absurdist premise literally, it reveals his megalomania, it's delivered with zero irony, and it's exceptionally quotable in four words. The economy is nearly perfect. This is the episode's standout moment — comparable to the 8.0 anchor but exceeding it in character integration and surprise.

jokes.text: The Harlem Globetrotters are gonna be there. The girl from Heroes is gonna take a shower. Now Jack is going to this party? This is nuts.
jokes.setup: The rumored party attractions keep escalating.
jokes.punchline: 'The girl from Heroes is gonna take a shower' — the rumor mill has degraded to voyeuristic specificity; someone is going to shower at a party.
jokes.explanation: The shower rumor is the best element here — by this point the party rumors have become so specific and random that someone showering is treated as an attraction. Good escalation.

jokes.text: I've called this meeting to discuss what happened last night at Kenneth's party.
jokes.setup: Kenneth calls a formal meeting the morning after.
jokes.punchline: The formality of 'I've called this meeting' — Kenneth treating a party disaster with corporate procedural gravity — is the joke, setting up the damage-assessment sequence.
jokes.explanation: Good structural setup for the post-party reckoning. Kenneth's formal gravity applied to a party is character-appropriate and sets the tone.

jokes.text: Y'all should be ashamed of yourselves. Mr. Lutz, you ate all my parakeet's medication.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is issuing formal rebukes to each party attendee.
jokes.punchline: Lutz ate a parakeet's medication — the first specific transgression is already deeply specific and weird.
jokes.explanation: The party accountability sequence is a great bit. Leading with 'Lutz ate my parakeet's medication' is an inspired opening — it's specific, bizarre, and immediately tells you this party was catastrophic. Good escalation setup.

jokes.text: And thanks to you, Sonny Crockett has been having seizures all morning.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has rebuked Lutz for eating the parakeet's medication.
jokes.punchline: The parakeet's name is Sonny Crockett — named after the Miami Vice character — and he's now seizing due to Lutz's drug consumption.
jokes.explanation: Excellent double joke. First, Kenneth's parakeet is named Sonny Crockett (Miami Vice), which is a characteristically Southern/nerdy Kenneth choice. Second, the formal name drop in this context ('Sonny Crockett has been having seizures') is delivered with the gravity of a medical update. The callback joke here is that the seizures are Lutz's fault. Highly quotable, strongly in character.

jokes.text: Mr. Hornberger, I would thank you to come pick up your wife at some point.
jokes.setup: Kenneth continues his formal rebukes.
jokes.punchline: Pete's wife Paula is still at Kenneth's apartment — presumably too wild to have left on her own.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Paula, who we know is sexually adventurous and chaotic, has apparently gotten loose at Kenneth's party and can't leave. 'I would thank you to come pick up your wife' is wonderfully formal Kenneth language.

jokes.text: Mr. Jordan, I saw you steal my sink.
jokes.setup: Kenneth continues his formal party rebukes.
jokes.punchline: Tracy stole Kenneth's sink — an entire household fixture. The specificity (not just something small but an entire sink) escalates the party damage.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. 'I saw you steal my sink' is beautifully absurd — the idea of someone physically removing a sink from an apartment at a party, and the flat tone of Kenneth reporting it, is inspired. The economy ('I saw you steal my sink' — six words) is near-perfect. The specificity of it being a SINK is what elevates this above 'I saw you steal something.'

jokes.text: Harlem Globetrotter... does that name mean nothing to you?
jokes.setup: Kenneth rebukes the Harlem Globetrotter who attended the party.
jokes.punchline: An actual Harlem Globetrotter apparently misbehaved at Kenneth's party, and Kenneth invokes their good-reputation brand against them — as if 'Harlem Globetrotter' carries the weight of a code of honor.
jokes.explanation: Great joke. The Harlem Globetrotters actually showed up (because of Tracy's ridiculous rumor), and one of them misbehaved so badly that Kenneth is invoking their brand reputation against them. Kenneth's sincere invocation of 'Harlem Globetrotter' as a moral standard is perfect character comedy. The callback payoff from the rumor sequence is satisfying.

jokes.text: And Ms. Lemon — I will have you know that before last night, I had never, ever seen Grizz or Dotcom cry.
jokes.setup: Kenneth continues his rebukes, reaching Liz.
jokes.punchline: Whatever Liz did was so bad that it made two large, presumably stoic men cry — and this is the worst thing Kenneth can say about it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The fact that Kenneth doesn't specify what Liz did — only its effect on Grizz and Dotcom — is the perfect withholding strategy. The idea that Grizz and Dotcom are big enough personalities that their tears are the ultimate measure of trauma is both funny and slightly disturbing. The understated delivery ('I will have you know') makes it land harder.

jokes.text: And Ms. Lemon. I will have you know that before last night, I had never, ever seen Grizz or Dotcom cry.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is cataloguing each person's party crimes; it's Liz's turn
jokes.punchline: Liz's offense was apparently so egregious that she made two large men named Grizz and Dotcom cry — and Kenneth has never seen this before
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke because it's entirely about what we DON'T see. What did Liz do? The unstated offense is funnier than anything that could be described. The specific detail of Grizz and Dotcom (Tracy's large, stoic associates) crying is perfect — these are not people you'd expect to cry, and Liz caused it. Kenneth's muted horror ('I will have you know') is the right register.

jokes.text: Congratulations. You were all present at Kenneth Parcell's last party ever.
jokes.setup: Kenneth has finished his formal rebukes.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's final verdict — no more parties, ever — delivered as a formal announcement with the weight of a corporate memo. The use of 'Congratulations' as an ironic opener is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The structure of the accountability sequence — each specific crime listed, building to this — is perfect, and the payoff lands with genuine weight. 'Congratulations' as a preamble to the worst news creates a tonal whiplash that's devastating and funny. The full name 'Kenneth Parcell's last party ever' adds formality and finality. High economy, exceptional character integration — Kenneth's earnest heartbreak expressed through rigid formality is perfect.

jokes.text: I may have gotten him here under false pretenses. / So I'm excited to see this trash-powered car of yours.
jokes.setup: Jack needs a new Greenzo after firing Jared; Al Gore appears
jokes.punchline: Gore thinks he's there to see a real GE innovation (a trash-powered car); he's actually been lured under false pretenses to be a corporate mascot
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the Al Gore sequence. The irony of Gore being manipulated by the same corporate machinery he opposes, delivered with Jack's casual admission of 'false pretenses,' is well-handled.

jokes.text: We met when Jack was an intern for Senator Ted Kennedy. Let me tell ya, Jack was the most liberal guy—
jokes.setup: Al Gore is reminiscing about how he and Jack know each other.
jokes.punchline: Jack frantically interrupts before Gore can reveal his liberal past — the joke is in the interruption and the implication that Jack's current right-wing persona was not always his identity.
jokes.explanation: Strong character joke — the implication that Jack Donaghy, arch-conservative corporate titan, was once a Kennedy liberal intern is a perfect bit of character subversion. The panic of the interruption sells it. Good character integration — the joke only works because we know exactly who Jack is now.

jokes.text: Al, we're with you on this whole planet thing. I mean, look at the set we built with the smiley-face earth and some green things.
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Al Gore of GE's environmental commitment.
jokes.punchline: Jack's evidence of environmental commitment is 'a smiley-face earth and some green things' — the most superficial possible set dressing presented as genuine conviction.
jokes.explanation: Good joke skewering corporate greenwashing — the 'smiley-face earth and some green things' is a perfect summation of shallow environmental PR. 'Green things' as a category is particularly funny.

jokes.text: Yes, or... you could put on a silly hat and tell the kids how outsourcing means cheaper toys at Christmas.
jokes.setup: Al Gore has proposed serious structural changes — CO2 taxes, congressional lobbying — as genuine environmental commitment.
jokes.punchline: Jack's counter-offer is that Gore wear a silly hat and spin outsourcing as a Christmas benefit for children — the most cynical possible reframing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent satire. Jack's reframing of outsourcing as 'cheaper toys at Christmas' is a perfect distillation of corporate spin logic — using children as a rhetorical shield for labor exploitation, delivered with complete sincerity. The 'silly hat' detail grounds it in the Greenzo aesthetic. Strong character integration — this is exactly how Jack thinks. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Back off, Jack! Or you'll be Greenzoed! You'll all be Greenzoed!
jokes.setup: Jared crashes the Today Show set to confront Jack and Al Gore.
jokes.punchline: 'You'll be Greenzoed' — the threat of being subjected to Greenzo's eco-madness, presented with the gravity of a real threat. The verb 'Greenzoed' is invented and absurd.
jokes.explanation: Fun escalation of the Greenzo arc — using his own name as a verb for a threat is a satisfying absurdist peak for the character. Good economy and commitment.

jokes.text: A whale is in trouble. I have to go.
jokes.setup: The chaos with Greenzo is unresolved; Jack is trying to apologize to Al Gore.
jokes.punchline: Gore receives what is presumably an alert on his phone and leaves with complete urgency — treating whale rescue as a higher priority than everything else happening.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's greatest moments and a 30 Rock classic. The economy is extraordinary — four words ('A whale is in trouble') communicate everything. Gore's deadpan delivery, the implication that he personally responds to whale emergencies, and the abrupt departure make this feel like real character-defining satire. It's a perfect joke: unexpected, character-perfect, economical, and quotable to the point of cultural resonance. Tied with joke 65 for episode best. Comparable in quality to the highest anchors.

jokes.text: Give it to me.
jokes.setup: Gore is leaving to help a whale; someone apparently offers him something.
jokes.punchline: Gore takes whatever is offered without breaking stride — complete commitment to the whale emergency.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Gore whale joke — the committed 'Give it to me' while exiting for a whale emergency extends the absurdity. Dependent on joke 80 for its impact.

jokes.text: Oh boy, okay. This earth is ruined! We gotta get a new one.
jokes.setup: The episode's environmental chaos has concluded.
jokes.punchline: Jack's final verdict — the earth is ruined, get a new one — is the ultimate statement of his resource-extraction philosophy: when one planet is used up, simply move on.
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing line. 'This earth is ruined! We gotta get a new one' is the logical conclusion of Jack's opening philosophy about draining resources. It's a callback that serves as the episode's thematic punchline — the entire Greenzo arc ends with Jack simply deciding to replace the planet. Highly quotable, exceptional economy, perfect character integration. Among the episode's very best.

tmdb_overview: It's time for Kenneth's annual house party, but he may be the only one excited about it. The soiree has only been attended by Liz in the past, so in order to get a better turnout Tracy spreads rumors that ultimately get out of hand.  Meanwhile, Jack deals with NBC's new environmentally-friendly mascot, whose new-found stardom goes to his head.
insight: Environmental satire escalates brilliantly—65 jokes in 22 minutes sustains absurdist pace throughout.
